contributions.headingText: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by germline pathogenic variants in NF1 predisposing to the development of benign and malignant tumours.

162200 Neurofibromatosis type 1; NF1

601321 Neurofibromatosis-Noonan syndrome; NFNS
<font color="red">Classification in progress, Data not available in this Beta</font>
Not recommended: von Recklinghausen disease; peripheral neurofibromatosis.
Tumours associated with NF1 are localized in the brain, central and peripheral nerves, and breast.

There are no specific clinical features of NF1-associated breast cancer (NF1-BC), although patients with deletions of the whole NF1 gene (so-called microdeletions), who tend to experience more-severe NF1-related disease, including a higher incidence of malignant tumours such as malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours, paradoxically appear to be at low risk of NF1-BC {30530636}. However, although NF1-BC can occur at any age, it tends to occur at younger ages and is more malignant {21694737;27931045}. Mammographic screening seems to be effective {36863889}.

NF1 has a prevalence of 1 case per 2000–3500 individuals, consistent across all populations studied {28230061}. NF1-BC occurs in both male and female patients, sometimes bilaterally, consistent with predisposition {16786042;14759722;27931045}. Both the absolute and relative risks of NF1-BC in female patients up to the age of 50 years are increased: 7.8–8.4% versus 2% in the general population, with standardized incidence ratios of 4.0–8.8 (see #48219Table 10.14).

NF1 is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in NF1 (17q11.2) {23496147;2134734;1946382;1946460}. A high proportion of cases are due to de novo variants. The expressivity and age-related penetrance are variable. There is evidence that NF1-BC is more likely in patients with pathogenic variants of NF1 that confer a gain of function {30530636}. This is consistent with a study of somatic NF1 mutations observed in sporadic cancers, in which breast cancer stands out as being the only type of malignancy in which amplification of NF1 is common (and, importantly, is independent of ERBB2 amplification) {28637487;30530636}.

Neurofibromin (NF1) is a large (2485 amino acids) cytoplasmic protein that primarily functions as a RAS-GAP {8499945}. The EVH1 domain of SPRED1 (the gene mutated in Legius syndrome) binds to neurofibromin (NF1) on both sides of the GAP-related domain and recruits neurofibromin (NF1) to the plasma membrane where it accelerates RAS inactivation {26635368;27313208}. Neurofibromin (NF1) forms a dimer, which creates two functional states with respect to RAS regulation {34707296}. It is predominantly expressed in neurons, Schwann cells, and oligodendrocytes. A potential direct functional link to ER signalling and modulation of the stromal microenvironment have recently been demonstrated in rat models {30182054;38799507}.
There are no specific macroscopic features associated with NF1-BC.

Breast cancers occurring in NF1 are mostly adenocarcinomas of no special type (NST), but lobular neoplasms also occur. Recent data have also shown an association with sporadic metaplastic carcinoma in which overrepresentation of somatic NF1 mutations was noted {30350370}.
No consistent features, such as positivity for ER, PR, or ERBB2 (HER2), have been noted for NF1-BC, but there is a lack of definitive evidence to exclude a relationship.

Essential: at least two of the following features:

Six or more café-au-lait macules (> 5 mm diameter in children, > 15 mm in adults) Axillary/inguinal freckling Two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform neurofibroma Optic pathway glioma Two or more iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules) or two or more choroidal abnormalities Distinctive bony abnormality (anterolateral bowing of the tibia, pseudarthrosis of a long bone, sphenoid dysplasia) Heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant with a variant allele fraction of 50% in apparently normal tissue Parent with NF1 (by the above criteria)

See #50771Table 10.15.
The staging of breast cancer in NF1 is the same as for sporadic breast cancer.

Given the increased risk of breast cancer in NF1, screening for breast cancer in women with NF1 may be advised. However, recent work showing that the risk of breast cancer may be higher in relation to specific NF1 variants, and that patients with whole gene deletions may be at reduced risk, indicates that generalizing the risk in individuals may be of limited utility; in the future, more-personalized variant-specific advice may be possible {30530636}.

NF1-BC tends to have a poorer prognosis, and this may be related to presentation at later stages, which is likely to be due in part to patients with NF1 often having learning difficulties, a well-recognized risk factor in late diagnosis {18956796;15801486}. Three human studies have reported increased mortality and unfavourable prognostic factors with NF1-BC {21694737;27931045;29926297}.
